name: Proximity bias
aliases: Out of sight, out of mind bias
statement: Managers reward the employees they can see, so office presence buys evaluation and advancement that equally good remote work does not.
meaning: Proximity bias is a term of hybrid-work commentary rather than of research psychology. A Crossref title search for the phrase returns electron-beam lithography, resist processing, magnetic thin films, investors' preference for shares in nearby firms, and a probability-judgement effect that its authors call novel. PubMed holds eight records with the phrase in the title or abstract, on video assistant referees, CRISPR editing, Arabic spatial deixis, affective metaphors in depression, primate hippocampal ripples, cochlear implant surgery and string pulling in dogs. None is the workplace construct. What the term points at is a chain of three claims. Managers see office workers more often than remote ones. Being seen produces favourable inferences about the worker. Those inferences reach pay and promotion. The middle claim has experimental support of its own. The last has been put to a randomised test twice, at the same Chinese travel firm, and the two results point in opposite directions.

origin.who: Nicholas Bloom, James Liang, John Roberts and Zhichun Jenny Ying
origin.note: No publication coining the name in its workplace sense was located. This is the randomised experiment the term's central claim is usually traced to, published online on 20 November 2014 and in the January 2015 issue. Where the exact phrase appears in indexed scholarship it usually means something else: semiconductor lithography since the 1990s, and investors' local bias, which carries a 2017 Springer monograph by Lindblom, Mavruk and Sjogren.

evidence:
Bloom, Liang, Roberts and Ying ran the experiment at Ctrip, a NASDAQ-listed Chinese travel agency. Of 996 employees in the Shanghai call centre's airfare and hotel departments, 503 said they were interested in working from home, and 249 met the eligibility conditions of six months' tenure, broadband and a private room. James Liang drew a ball from an urn at a public ceremony to decide that even birthdates went into treatment, giving 131 home workers and 118 controls. Treatment meant working at home four days a week and in the office on the fifth. Over nine months, home workers' performance rose 13 percent, 9 percentage points of it from more minutes logged in per shift and 4 from more calls per minute. Their attrition halved.

Promotions were tracked over the 22 months from 6 December 2010 to 30 September 2012, counting promotion to team leader or a move to a more advanced job function. Forty of the 249 were promoted, a rate of 15.9 percent: 17 in the treatment group and 23 in the control group. A probit with no other regressors gives a marginal effect of working from home of -0.065 with a standard error of 0.047, which the authors read as no overall effect on promotion. Adding performance during the experiment turns the estimate to -0.087 with a standard error of 0.048, significant at 10 percent. Adding demographics gives -0.085, and a specification interacting home working with performance gives a level effect of -0.091, significant at 5 percent, alongside an interaction of -0.105 significant at 10 percent. The authors offer three readings of the pattern, and the first is the one the term borrows: home-based employees were out of sight and out of mind, so supervisors noticed their performance less. The second is that home workers had fewer chances to build the interpersonal skills a managerial job needs. The third is that they did not want promotion, because it meant returning to the office.

Elsbach, Cable and Sherman supply the middle link. They distinguish expected passive face time, being seen during normal hours, from extracurricular passive face time, being seen outside them, and report that observers infer 'dependable' from the first and 'committed' from the second. Their experimental study finds the inferences are made spontaneously, without intent or awareness. Golden and Eddleston tested the last link outside the laboratory, matching 405 employees to corporate records of promotion and salary growth. Telecommuters and non-telecommuters did not differ in number of promotions, and telecommuters had lower salary growth. Extent of telecommuting was negatively related to both. Context moved the result: extensive telecommuters got more promotions where telecommuting was normative and where they did more supplemental work, and better salary growth where they also had more face-to-face contact with their supervisor.

replication.headline: Two randomised trials at the same Chinese travel firm disagree. The 2010 call-centre experiment found a promotion penalty conditional on performance; the 2021 hybrid experiment found no promotion difference across four review periods.
replication.detail:
Bloom, Han and Liang ran the second experiment at Trip.com, the same company under its later name. On 27 July 2021 the firm surveyed 1,612 eligible engineering, marketing and finance employees in its Shanghai airfare and IT divisions, excluding interns and staff on probation. Randomisation was again by odd and even birthday within the month. Treatment carried the option, not the obligation, to work from home on Wednesday or Friday. Quit rates fell by about a third. Promotions were followed through four six-month review periods to June 2023, on samples of 1,522, 1,378, 1,314 and 1,283 as the original sample shrank through attrition. The treatment minus control differences in promotions were -0.86, 0.12, -0.51 and -0.99, with standard errors of 1.34, 0.85, 1.12 and 1.02 and P values of 0.509, 0.892, 0.651 and 0.328. The authors report no evidence of a difference in promotions over the two years, overall or in any major subgroup, and equivalence tests against bounds of half a letter grade rejected any meaningful effect on performance grades in all four periods.

The two experiments differ in more than their result. Ctrip's treatment was four days at home for call-centre staff on individual performance pay; Trip.com's was an option to take two days at home for graduate professionals. The Ctrip promotion estimate that carries the penalty is also the one that conditions on performance measured after randomisation, and the authors flag the distinction themselves, noting that their unconditional column estimates a total derivative and the conditional column a partial one. The unconditional comparison, the one the lottery licenses, is not significant in either study.

study.cite: Bloom, N., Han, R., & Liang, J. (2024). Hybrid working from home improves retention without damaging performance. Nature, 630(8018), 920-925.

limits:
The name has no located research base, and that is the first limit. Searches covered Crossref bibliographic and title queries, including a title query restricted to work published before 2017, PubMed title and abstract search, Semantic Scholar and web search. Nothing empirical about workplace evaluation was found under the term. The nearest thing to an academic treatment located is a chapter titled 'Supporting DEI and Addressing Proximity Bias' in a 2023 practitioner book, whose Crossref record lists no author and which was not read.

Both randomised experiments are the same firm in one city, run by overlapping author teams, one of whom co-founded the company. Neither was designed to measure an evaluator's bias. They measure what happened to promotions, which is the outcome the term predicts and not the mechanism it names. No study was found that varies an evaluator's exposure to a worker and measures the resulting rating while holding output fixed.

The Ctrip figures were read from the published article and cross-checked against the March 2013 CEP discussion paper. That check mattered: the text layer of the published PDF drops the minus signs from the treatment row of Table IX, so the coefficients extract as positive and contradict the paper's own prose. The working paper's Table 9 carries the signs, and the shared values of 0.087, 0.085 and 0.091 identify the rows as the same. The '50 percent' reduction stated in both introductions could not be derived from any table read here, and it is reported below as the authors' summary rather than as a table entry.

Golden and Eddleston's article sits behind an Elsevier paywall that returned HTTP 403. Its design and results here come from the publisher abstract as carried by Semantic Scholar, which reports no effect sizes or intervals. Elsbach, Cable and Sherman is described from the abstract carried by Crossref; the sample sizes and effect sizes of its experimental study were not obtained. Gajendran and Harrison's meta-analysis of 46 telecommuting studies covering 12,883 employees was checked as a possible source on career outcomes. The abstract lists autonomy, work-family conflict, workplace relationships, job satisfaction, performance, turnover intent and role stress, and no career-advancement outcome, so it is not used above for that purpose.
misreadings:
The commonest claim is that the Ctrip experiment showed home workers were half as likely to be promoted. The paper's introduction does say that, conditional on performance, home working was associated with reduced promotion rates of about 50 percent. Three things get dropped in the retelling. The randomised comparison, treatment against control with nothing else in the regression, is not statistically significant. The penalty appears only once performance during the experiment is held constant, and at that point the estimate is significant at 10 percent, which the authors call weakly significant. In raw counts, 17 of 131 home workers and 23 of 118 controls were promoted.

The Ctrip home workers were not remote. They worked at home four days a week and came into the office on the fifth, and they were volunteers, drawn from the half of the department that wanted the arrangement.

The same firm's later experiment is rarely mentioned alongside the first. It is larger, it covers professional rather than call-centre work, it follows promotions for two years, and it finds nothing. A claim that the evidence shows a promotion penalty for remote work has to explain why the better-powered trial at the same employer does not.

Face-time research is often cited as if it measured outcomes. Elsbach, Cable and Sherman measured inferences about traits, made by observers about a person they had seen. Whether those inferences change a pay rise is a separate question their study did not ask.

Proximity does have measured effects that are not evaluator favouritism. Emanuel, Harrington and Pallais studied software engineers at a Fortune 500 firm from 2019 to 2024, using office closures and later return-to-office mandates as shocks. Sitting near teammates raised coding feedback by 18.3 percent and improved code quality, with gains concentrated among younger and less-tenured engineers, while experienced engineers wrote less code when seated near their teams. That is a story about who receives training, not about who a manager likes, and the two imply different remedies. Their paper is an NBER working paper and has not been peer reviewed.

The last confusion is the name itself. Hong, Longoni and Morwitz introduced 'proximity bias' in the Journal of Consumer Psychology for something unrelated: across six experiments with a combined 4,007 participants, a positive outcome was judged more likely when near than distant and a negative outcome less likely, which they attribute to wishful thinking. Lindblom, Mavruk and Sjogren use the same phrase for investors overweighting nearby firms. Wikipedia's article on proximity bias names no coiner and grounds the idea in Segal's 1974 study of Maryland state police trainees, whose dormitory rooms and classroom seats were assigned alphabetically and whose friendships followed the alphabet. That is a finding about who becomes friends, not about who gets promoted.

sources.text: Bloom, N., Liang, J., Roberts, J., & Ying, Z. J. (2015). Does working from home work? Evidence from a Chinese experiment. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 130(1), 165-218. Full text read. Note that the published PDF's text layer drops the minus signs from the treatment row of Table IX.

Bloom, N., Liang, J., Roberts, J., & Ying, Z. J. (2013). Does working from home work? Evidence from a Chinese experiment. CEP Discussion Paper No. 1194. Read in full and used to confirm the signs of the promotion coefficients, which its Table 9 prints as negative.
Bloom, N., Han, R., & Liang, J. (2024). Hybrid working from home improves retention without damaging performance. Nature, 630(8018), 920-925. Read in full from the PubMed Central copy.

Golden, T. D., & Eddleston, K. A. (2020). Is there a price telecommuters pay? Examining the relationship between telecommuting and objective career success. Journal of Vocational Behavior, 116, 103348. Paywalled; described from the publisher abstract as carried by Semantic Scholar.

Elsbach, K. D., Cable, D. M., & Sherman, J. W. (2010). How passive 'face time' affects perceptions of employees: Evidence of spontaneous trait inference. Human Relations, 63(6), 735-760. Described from the abstract carried by Crossref.

Gajendran, R. S., & Harrison, D. A. (2007). The good, the bad, and the unknown about telecommuting: Meta-analysis of psychological mediators and individual consequences. Journal of Applied Psychology, 92(6), 1524-1541. Abstract read at PubMed; checked for career outcomes and none are listed there.

Emanuel, N., Harrington, E., & Pallais, A. (2023, revised 2026). The power of proximity to coworkers. NBER Working Paper 31880. Abstract read from the working paper PDF; not peer reviewed. A text search of the PDF returns no occurrence of the word 'promotion'.

Hong, J. S., Longoni, C., & Morwitz, V. (2024). Proximity bias: Interactive effect of spatial distance and outcome valence on probability judgments. Journal of Consumer Psychology, 34(1), 18-34. Described from the abstract carried by Crossref. Cited as a namespace clash, not as evidence for the workplace claim.
Lindblom, T., Mavruk, T., & Sjogren, S. (2017). Proximity Bias in Investors' Portfolio Choice. Springer International Publishing. Cited as the established scholarly use of the phrase; not read.

Supporting DEI and Addressing Proximity Bias. In Thrive with a Hybrid Workplace (2023), 175-182. The nearest thing to an academic treatment of the workplace term located in these searches. The Crossref record lists no author; the chapter was not read.

Segal, M. W. (1974). Alphabet and attraction: An unobtrusive measure of the effect of propinquity in a field setting. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 30(5), 654-657. Named because Wikipedia's proximity bias article rests the idea on it; not read for this entry.
Wikipedia, 'Proximity bias'. Checked for a coinage claim; the article names no coiner. An index, not a source for any finding on this page.
